title: Low Frequency Gravitational Wave Detection with Gravito-Magnetism
abstract: The detection of gravitational waves in the low-frequency band (10 nHz to 1 micro-Hz) using inner solar system proof masses is severely limited by Newtonian gravity gradient noise (GGN) sourced by the asteroid belt. In this paper, we propose a novel detection concept that exploits the relativistic nature of gravitational waves to break the degeneracy between the signal and the asteroid GGN background. The non-relativistic motion of asteroids dominantly sources gravito-electric fields, with velocity suppressed gravito-magnetic components. Relativistic gravitational waves produce gravito-electric and gravito-magnetic components of equal magnitude. We propose detecting the gravito-magnetic component of low frequency gravitational waves using the Lorentz acceleration of test bodies. The measurement of this Lorentz acceleration is metrologically possible due to the fact that expected astrophysical sources of low frequency gravitational waves have considerably higher characteristic strains than the strains typically expected at higher frequencies. We show that this measurement allows for unambiguous extraction of the gravitational wave signal from the gravity gradient noise in a three satellite constellation. The gravito-magnetic measurement still requires a proof mass that is well isolated from non-gravitational noise. We propose the use of atom interferometers to serve as such a pristine inertial reference.
summary: This work proposes a novel method to detect low-frequency gravitational waves by measuring the gravitomagnetic component, which allows separation from dominant gravity gradient noise. The technique requires a three-satellite constellation and proposes using atom interferometers to provide the necessary ultra-stable inertial reference for the proof mass. This combines advanced general relativity concepts with cutting-edge AMO metrology.
main_problem: Detecting low-frequency gravitational waves (10 nHz to 1 $\mu$Hz) is severely limited by Newtonian gravity gradient noise (GGN) from the asteroid belt.
main_result: By exploiting the relativistic nature of gravitational waves to measure the gravitomagnetic component via Lorentz acceleration, the signal can be unambiguously extracted from the GGN background using a three-satellite constellation.
method: The authors propose using a three-satellite constellation to measure discrete double time differences in laser pulse arrival times, combined with the use of atom interferometers as a pristine inertial reference.
model_or_system: The system involves three satellites in elliptical orbits around the Sun, measuring time-of-arrival of laser pulses. The proposed enhancement uses atom interferometers to stabilize a macroscopic proof mass, mimicking LISA-like setups.
key_observables: The gravitomagnetic component of gravitational waves, measured via the Lorentz acceleration ($\vec{v} 	imes \vec{B}_{	ext{gravito}}$) on test bodies, and the discrete double time difference ($\Delta^2	au_{jk}$) between satellite laser pulses.
important_parameters: Low-frequency band (10 nHz to 1 $\mu$Hz); required interrogation time $T \sim 10^4$ s; target acceleration sensitivity $\sim 10^{-21} 	ext{ m/s}^2/\sqrt{	ext{Hz}}$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the weak field limit and relies on the ability to use atom interferometers to provide an inertial reference stable enough for long interrogation times.

paper_structure: The paper first establishes the fundamental concept of using gravitomagnetism to overcome GGN noise. It then details the measurement protocol using a three-satellite constellation based on time-of-arrival measurements. Finally, it discusses the necessary technological upgrade using atom interferometers to achieve the required inertial stability.
why_interesting: The integration of ultra-cold atom interferometry (a core AMO technique) to stabilize the inertial reference for gravitational wave detection is highly relevant. It pushes the boundaries of precision measurement by requiring control over quantum systems (atoms) to measure classical spacetime perturbations.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The three-satellite measurement constellation in solar orbit. Satellite i serves as the master clock to synchronize the array. The deputy satellites exchange laser pulses at designated global times T, T + τ, and T + 2τ to measure the discrete double time difference ∆2τ. The multiple baselines are mathematically required to invert the signal matrix and simultaneously canceling higher-order gravity gradient noise from the asteroid belt.

Figure 2: The hybrid atom-interferometer proof mass concept. A sun shield creates a 30-meter dark vacuum region behind the satellite. Ultra-cold atoms produced in the satellite are sent to this region. Laser pulses from the satellite, along with their reflections from the retro-reflector, are used to execute Mach-Zender π/2 −π −π/2 sequences to measure non-gravitational accelerations, which are fed back to fully stabilize the central macroscopic proof mass. We need such a setup along each measurement axis - thus, two such interferometers for each satellite.
